cards.rueckseite: 80% **occipital**, 15% frontoethmoidal (sincipital), rest basal. Associated with spina bifida, split cord, Chiari II/III, Klippel–Feil, Dandy–Walker. Basal forms can present later with CSF leak. Treatment: excision with watertight dural closure ± hydrocephalus treatment.

**Chiari I:** young adults, tonsillar herniation; ~25% with skeletal anomalies (basilar invagination, Klippel–Feil, C1 assimilation); hydrocephalus ~25%; suboccipital headache worse with **cough/Valsalva**.
**Chiari II:** infants, **myelomeningocele in 100%**, hindbrain anomalies, aqueductal stenosis, lacunar skull, low torcula; hydrocephalus ~90%.
Syrinx in ~50% of both.
From above down: **hydrocephalus first**, then **posterior fossa decompression** with expansile duraplasty (~80% improve), the **syrinx** usually resolves afterwards.

Cystic enlargement of the **4th ventricle**, **vermian agenesis/hypoplasia**, enlarged posterior fossa (high torcula). Hydrocephalus in ~80%, other anomalies in ⅔. Treatment: shunting (cyst ± ventricle). ~50% normal intelligence.
Mainly cosmetic; raised ICP in ~10%. Strip craniectomy / cranial vault remodeling; main risk is **blood loss** needing transfusion. **Positional plagiocephaly**: repositioning ± helmet.

**GCS ≤ 8 with abnormal CT** (hematoma, contusion, swelling), or GCS ≤ 8 with **normal CT** and ≥ 2 of:
- age > 40
- motor posturing (uni-/bilateral)
- systolic BP < 90 mmHg

cards.text: Elevated ICP develops in {{c1::3%}} of mild, {{c2::10–12%}} of moderate and {{c3::~50%}} of severe head injuries.
Kocher's point (EVD): {{c1::1–2 cm anterior to the coronal suture}} and {{c2::2–3 cm lateral to the midline}}, usually right side.
Treat ICP if {{c1::> 20 mmHg}} for more than 5 minutes or CPP {{c2::< 60 mmHg}}.
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 621. Brain Trauma Foundation 4th ed.: treat ICP > 22 mmHg, target CPP 60–70 mmHg.

cards.rueckseite:
1. Head up 30°, neck straight, no jugular compression
2. Analgesia/sedation
3. Avoid hypoxia and hypercarbia (intubate if GCS ≤ 8, normocapnia; hyperventilation only briefly)
4. MAP > 90 / CPP ≥ 60
5. Treat hyponatremia, fever, hyperglycemia
6. CSF drainage via EVD
7. Mannitol / hypertonic saline (serum osm < 320 mOsm/L)
8. Surgery: evacuation, decompressive craniectomy
9. Barbiturate coma to burst suppression

Early seizures (< 7 days) in 4–25%. Give anticonvulsants for **1 week only** (prevents early, not late seizures). Risk factors: GCS < 10, cortical contusion, hematoma, penetrating injury, depressed fracture, seizure within 24 h.

- Open fracture with dural tear (depression > 1 cm, CSF leak, pneumocephalus)
- Significant mass effect or underlying hematoma
- Cosmetic deformity (forehead)
- Displaced posterior table of frontal sinus
Conservative if over a major venous sinus. Elevation does **not** reduce late seizure risk.
~1% of skull fractures, mainly young children. **Dural tear** with entrapped arachnoid/brain prevents healing → enlarging pulsatile mass. Treatment: **craniotomy with duraplasty**.

cards.vorderseite: Traumatic CSF leak: natural history and management
cards.rueckseite: 3% of head injuries. 70–85% stop spontaneously within 2 weeks. Meningitis 5–10%. Persistent (> 5–7 days): **lumbar drain**, then surgical repair if it fails. **Prophylactic antibiotics not recommended**.
Gunshot wounds: mortality ~90%. **Leave protruding objects in place** until in the OR. **Angiography** if a major artery or sinus is at risk. Debride/remove fragments only if mass effect.

cards.vorderseite: Epidural hematoma: source and classic course
cards.rueckseite: Arterial in 40–50% (**middle meningeal artery**), also venous/diploic. Skull fracture in 85%. Classic: brief LOC → **lucid interval** → deterioration, **ipsilateral blown pupil**, contralateral hemiparesis. Mortality ~20% (10% if treated early).
Mass compresses the **contralateral cerebral peduncle** against the tentorial edge → **ipsilateral hemiparesis**: a false localizing sign.

Bridging vein tear or cortical laceration; more underlying brain injury than EDH, usually **no lucid interval**. Anticoagulation raises risk 10–30×. Mortality > 50% (> 80% if > 65 y). Classic study: halved mortality if evacuated **within 4 hours**. Treatment: craniotomy.
Elderly (mean 65), risk factors trauma, alcohol, seizures, coagulopathy. **Burr hole drainage ± subdural drain** (~85% success); craniotomy for loculated/recurrent cases.
Coup/contrecoup on bony prominences (frontal, temporal, occipital poles). Often **enlarge/coalesce in the first 48–72 h** → repeat CT. Manage ICP, consider early evacuation.
